analysis.one_liner: Lets TV networks reach half the national audience and ends the ban on newspapers owning TV stations.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let TV networks own stations reaching 50% of U.S. households (up from 35%) and ended the newspaper-TV ownership ban, never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have raised the cap on how much of the national TV audience a single company's stations can reach, from 35% to 50%, and possibly higher. It also would have wiped out the rule that keeps a company from owning both a newspaper and a TV station in the same area, ending that rule by default on December 31, 1999 unless the FCC voted to keep it. The main beneficiaries would be the large broadcast networks and big newspaper chains, which could then buy many more stations and papers.
analysis.who_benefits: The major national TV networks (the companies already bumping against the 35% cap) could buy more stations and reach up to half — or more — of all U.S. viewers. Newspaper publishers and broadcasters could own both a paper and a TV or radio station in the same market, opening up a new wave of cross-ownership deals. Media holding companies would gain a larger pool of properties to buy and merge.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Big TV networks and newspaper chains

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the room to grow: the national audience-reach cap for TV station owners would go from 35% to 50% of U.S. households, so the big networks could buy and run roughly 15 more percentage points' worth of stations nationwide.
The bill would let the FCC raise the cap even beyond 50% if it decided that served the public interest, leaving the door open to near-unlimited national reach.

It would end the newspaper/broadcast cross-ownership rule by default after December 31, 1999 — the rule would vanish unless the FCC affirmatively reinstated it before January 1, 2000 — letting newspaper publishers buy stations (and broadcasters buy papers) in the same market.

analysis.who_pays: Viewers of local news would bear the cost if the bill passed: ownership limits exist to keep a few companies from controlling what local stations report, and each consolidation wave leaves fewer independent owners deciding local coverage. Independent station owners and smaller station groups would also face buyouts by the expanded networks, and newsroom jobs tend to be cut when two formerly separate local outlets merge under one owner.
analysis.who_pays_short: Local news viewers and independent station owners

drawbacks.text: Raising the reach cap to 50% would allow one company to own stations reaching half of all American TV households, concentrating decisions about local news and political advertising in a handful of boardrooms.

The cross-ownership rule would not be replaced with anything — it would simply expire on January 1, 2000 unless the FCC managed to reinstate it in the final weeks of 1999 — so the default outcome was elimination with no substitute safeguards.

The bill's own findings rest on the claim that cable and the Internet now provide 'abundant alternative' sources of news, but the bill does nothing to require that local broadcast outlets stay locally owned; an honest supporter would have to concede the rules being swept away predated the Internet and had never been reexamined on their merits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go almost entirely to large media companies, which would gain the ability to buy far more stations and combine newspapers with broadcast outlets. The bill offers the public only a theory — that cable and the Internet make ownership limits obsolete — while the concrete effect is fewer independent owners of local news sources. The costs to local news diversity are real and would fall on everyone; the gains are concentrated in a handful of boardrooms.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate Commerce Committee — chaired by its own sponsor — and the committee never held a vote on it before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator John McCain introduced the bill on September 13, 1999, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
No senator ever signed on as a cosponsor — the bill had zero cosponsors for its entire life.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; that referral was the last thing that ever happened to the bill.

The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill died in committee, so the 35% national reach cap and the newspaper/broadcast cross-ownership rule stayed in place at least through that Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Viewers of local news came out ahead for the time being, because the ownership limits that keep national networks and newspaper chains from consolidating local stations survived another two years. The big broadcast networks and newspaper publishers did not get the expanded buying power they sought from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Local-news viewers, at least for then

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor: introduced the bill, delivered introductory remarks, and sent it to the Commerce Committee he chaired — which then took no further action on it.

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out — no markup, no vote, no hearing in the record before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its only sponsor was a Republican, it attracted zero cosponsors of either party, and no opposition ever went on the record.

industries.industry: Broadcast television networks and large station groups
industries.note: The bill would have let the national networks expand from reaching 35% to 50% (or more) of U.S. TV households, fueling a wave of station buyouts. Their gain comes directly from owning more of the local stations Americans rely on for news.

Ending the newspaper/broadcast cross-ownership rule would let newspaper chains buy TV and radio stations in their own markets — and broadcasters buy papers — combining formerly independent local news outlets under one owner.

industries.industry: Independent and locally owned TV stations
industries.note: Smaller station groups would face much larger network buyers flushed with new acquisition room, and the independent local voices the ownership caps were designed to protect would be the first candidates for buyout.
